reason: Typology pulls and the arithmetic refuses. Nine of the twelve ask to live ‘unto the age of man’ (28:2) and are told they shall come to Christ ‘after that ye are seventy and two years old’ (28:3). The King James Bible has exactly one verse fixing the age of man — Psalm 90:10, ‘The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years’ — and it is the obvious source for a promise pegged to a human lifespan. But the Book of Mormon’s number is seventy-two, which is neither of Psalm 90:10’s two figures, and it shares not one word with the verse: no ‘threescore’, no ‘days of our years’, no ‘labour and sorrow’. A borrowing that adopted the psalm’s idea would have adopted its round number, which is the whole point of the psalm’s number. Recorded so that a reader who reaches for Psalm 90 is told the catalogue reached for it too and put it down.

sharedText: and said unto them, What will ye
reason: A seven-word run and the longest in the chapter, and it is the wrong Matthew 26 verse. Matthew 26:15 is Judas at the chief priests: ‘And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you?’ 3 Nephi 28:4 is Christ turning to the three: ‘and said unto them, What will ye that I should do unto you?’ The senses are inverted at every point — in Matthew the speaker is the betrayer, the addressees are the buyers, and the question is what he will be paid; in 3 Nephi the speaker is the one about to be departed from, the addressees are his disciples, and the question is what he will give. The run is the KJV’s ordinary formula for introducing direct speech plus two words of an interrogative, and the real source of the sentence is the question of Matthew 20:32 and Mark 10:51 in the setting of Mark 10:36, where the link is filed. Worth the entry because Matthew 26 does supply this chapter: 28:35 takes ‘if he had not been born’ from Matthew 26:24, nine verses further on, and a reader who notices that will want to know whether we considered 26:15. We did, and it is coincidence.

A five-word run scoring 2.00, and ‘the kingdom of my father’ is the phrase a Christian text uses for heaven without needing a source. Its one KJV occurrence is Ziba slandering Mephibosheth to David — ‘To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father’ — a lie told to steal an estate during Absalom’s revolt, and it is the only sentence in the King James Bible where the phrase appears. Nothing whatever connects it to a promise of the kingdom made to disciples who will not taste of death. The verse’s real borrowings are from 1 Corinthians 15:52-53 and they are filed at 28:8; this candidate ranked only because the KJV happens to have had one occasion to write the phrase and it was a usurper’s.

A five-word run and pure connective tissue. Numbers 31:5 is a muster roll — ‘there were delivered out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand of every tribe’ — where ‘delivered’ means handed over for service, not rescued. The Book of Mormon’s sense is rescue, and the verse’s real link is to Psalm 71:20, whose ‘depths of the earth’ is a KJV singleton and is filed at 28:20.

Four words of KJV boilerplate for priestly service; Numbers 1:50 is the appointment of the Levites over the tabernacle and its vessels, and what they minister unto is the tabernacle itself. The verse’s adjudicated link is the Revelation 14:6 formula that follows in the same clause.

sharedText: the Father in the name of
reason: A six-word run that is the standing Christian formula for prayer and thanksgiving, used throughout the Book of Mormon and throughout the New Testament; Ephesians 5:20 ranked only because its particular arrangement of the words is uncommon. Nothing else of Ephesians 5 is present. The distinctive contact in this verse is ‘as the angels of God’, a KJV singleton at Matthew 22:30, and the link is filed there.

Cross-reference, not a rejection. ‘Yea, even among the Gentiles shall there be a great and marvellous work wrought by them’ is Isaiah 29:14’s ‘a marvellous work and a wonder’, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse and which the Book of Mormon has been quoting since 1 Nephi; within 3 Nephi it is adjudicated at 21:9, where the Gentiles and the marvellous work stand in the same sentence as here. This is the narrator reusing a formula already established in his own book (ADJUDICATING §4), so the row is not written twice. The 1830 text spells it ‘marvellous’ at 28:31, 28:32 and 28:33, and ‘judgement’ at 28:31, 28:32 and 28:40, both KJV spellings modernised in 1920 — the first edition shows the borrowing more plainly than the current text does. A reader arriving at 28:32 should be sent to 3 Nephi 21:9.

sharedText: their bodies, that they might not
reason: The best trap in the chapter, because it is the right book and the wrong verse. Daniel 3 genuinely stands behind 28:21 — three men thrice cast into a furnace and unharmed — so a six-word run out of Daniel 3:28 looks like confirmation. It is not. Nebuchadnezzar’s sentence is about what Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego did before the fire: they ‘yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God’, an act of defiant obedience with the body offered up. 3 Nephi 28:38 is about what was done to the three Nephites afterwards: ‘there was a change wrought upon their bodies, that they might not suffer pain nor sorrow’, a divine alteration with the body received. The shared string is a possessive noun plus the KJV’s commonest purpose clause, and the two ‘might nots’ govern opposite things — refusal to serve, inability to suffer. The verse’s real source is 1 Corinthians 15:51-53, filed at 28:8 and recurring here, at 28:37, 28:39 and 28:40.
